## Dissertation: variational Bayes for sparse and functional regression

Bayesian variable selection with spike-and-slab priors gives a probability that each predictor
belongs in the model. Markov chain Monte Carlo is slow when there are thousands of predictors,
so variational Bayes (VB) is used instead. Standard VB has two weak points in this setting: its
results depend strongly on the prior settings, and its predictions are often poorly calibrated,
i.e. they are biased toward the mean. My dissertation, with Dr. Alexander McLain, develops VB
methods that stay fast and fix these problems.

1. **Parameter expanded VB** for spike-and-slab linear regression. Preprint on Research Square;
   under review at *Statistics and Computing*. Software: [`spexvb`](software.qmd) on CRAN.
2. **Parameter exploded VB** for sparse high-dimensional linear regression. In preparation.
3. **VB for scalar-on-function regression.** In progress. The predictor is a curve, such as a
   day of accelerometer data, expanded in a basis. This project carries the ideas of the first
   two projects to functional predictors.

### The problem and the first result

The first figure below shows the calibration problem with simulated data. In panel (a),
the predictions from standard VB are pulled toward zero, because the points lie on a flatter
line than the 45° line. In panel (b), the calibration coefficient α~c~ (black line; α~c~ ≈ 1
means good calibration) and the MSE (gray line) both change with the prior precision τ~b~. So,
the user of standard VB must choose τ~b~ well to get good predictions.

Our method, `spexvb`, adds parameter expansion to VB. The second figure compares how much
the test-set MSE changes across five values of τ~b~. We see that the range for `spexvb` (red)
is much smaller than for `sparsevb` (black), the standard VB method, in every scenario. So,
`spexvb` depends much less on the prior setting.

### Methods and data
The methods are evaluated with factorial simulation studies on a high-performance computing
cluster, and applied to genomic and wearable data.

## Wearable and accelerometer data

- **Clustering 24-hour physical activity in young children.** We clustered hourly activity
  curves of children 6 to 36 months old with model-based functional clustering.
  *Pediatric Exercise Science*, 2025 (first author).
- **Non-wear imputation in GGIR.** We measured the bias of GGIR's non-wear imputation by
  imposing real non-wear patterns on complete wrist accelerometer recordings. Along the way,
  two of my fixes were merged into the GGIR package.
- **Walking and cognition in Parkinson's disease.** Longitudinal mixed models of changes in
  walking and cognition by motor subtype. *Parkinsonism & Related Disorders*, 2026 (first
  author).

## High-dimensional mixed models

- `lmmprobe` fits sparse high-dimensional linear mixed models with a partitioned empirical
  Bayes ECM algorithm, developed by Dr. Anja Zgodic and co-authors (*Statistics and Computing*,
  2025). My contribution was to the software: I optimized the R package by rewriting its core
  routines in C++ with OpenMP.

## Before the Ph.D.

From 2018 to 2021 I was the biostatistician of the research office at Hospital Universitario
San Ignacio in Bogotá. I built clinical prediction models (emergency room mortality, high-flow
nasal cannula failure in COVID-19 pneumonia), designed patient registries in REDCap, and
co-authored papers in cardiology, infectious disease, and pulmonology. Before that I spent
about seven years in banking and consulting, building credit scoring and money-laundering
risk models.
